title: Images as numerical grids
goals: Encode and reconstruct a small image using an explicit grid convention
Explain why pixel counts alone cannot recover an arrangement
Distinguish numerical image data from a model's interpretation of that data

prerequisite.prompt: Two thresholds can agree on all fitting examples but disagree on a new input. Does zero fitting error identify one uniquely correct rule?
prerequisite.answer: No. The fitting examples may not distinguish the rules, and agreement on those examples does not settle every unseen case.

vocabulary: One position in a digital image grid with a recorded value or values
A convention for representing information with symbols or numbers
The number of positions in an image grid, often given as width by height
Where elements are located relative to one another
A meaning or category assigned to a representation using a rule, model or human judgment

lesson.title: Agree on the code before reading it

blocks.text: Imagine sending a small black-and-white sign using only numbers. We can divide the sign into a grid, record 1 for a black square and 0 for a white square, and read each row from left to right, starting at the top. The receiver needs the width, height and these conventions to reconstruct the same arrangement.

A pixel is a position with a recorded value. In our simplified binary image, one value selects black or white. Other image formats can record brightness levels or multiple colour channels. The convention 1 means black belongs to this exercise; it is not a universal rule for every digital image.

Encoding a picture does not recognise what it depicts. A program can store or display the numbers without calling the image a letter, an arrow or a person. Interpretation is another operation, just as displaying a book title was different from reading the entire book in Week 2.

lesson.title: Read a grid in a fixed order

blocks.title: A three by three binary image
blocks.key: Read rows top to bottom. Within each row read left to right. 1 is black and 0 is white.
blocks.caption: The image has width 3 and height 3, so it contains 9 pixels. Five are black. The row records preserve where those five black pixels occur.

blocks.text: The first row is 0,1,0, so only its middle pixel is black. The second row is 1,1,1, so all three are black. The third row repeats the first. This reconstructs the displayed cross-like pattern under our convention.

A flattened record would be 0,1,0,1,1,1,0,1,0. Without the grid dimensions, the same nine values could also be drawn in one row of nine. Keep the shape information with the values. Width times height counts pixels; it does not tell us their contents.

Suppose we discard the row records and retain only black pixel count=5. That count matches the cross, but it also matches rows 1,1,1 then 1,1,0 then 0,0,0. The second arrangement fills the top row and two positions below it. Both have five black pixels and nine pixels in total, yet they are different images.

rows: Five positions are black under this code
Dimensions and all three ordered rows
The full binary grid under this convention
What a viewer or model will call the picture

blocks.text: A pixel count can still be a useful feature for some tasks. For example, it can separate empty grids from grids with at least one mark. But it cannot separate every shape. To judge a feature, ask whether it retains the distinctions required by the task.

lesson.title: Reconstruct and check an unfamiliar image

blocks.text: Use width 3, height 2 and rows 1,0,1 then 0,1,0. Draw two rows of three squares and fill exactly the positions marked 1. Check by reading your drawing back into numbers. A round trip from code to drawing to code can reveal a swapped row or a missed pixel.

blocks.label: Draw the two by three image, write its black-pixel count and explain why saying only three black pixels would be insufficient

blocks.text: If an image classifier mislabels a picture, first inspect the input representation. Was the width correct? Were the rows reversed? Did the program use the intended colour convention? A later classifier cannot reliably repair every mistake in how its input was prepared.

lesson.title: More pixels do not settle every question

blocks.text: Higher resolution offers more positions for recording detail, but it does not guarantee a useful image. A larger blurry image can still hide a feature, and a cropped image can omit it entirely. A model's label also depends on what it was fitted to distinguish and the conditions represented in its examples.

Keep claims at the right stage. These nine values encode this grid is a reconstruction claim. This grid depicts a plus sign is an interpretation. This sign tells a person what to do adds context and authority. One does not automatically establish the others.

blocks.label: Can two different three by three images have the same black-pixel count? Explain with a specific arrangement change

workbook.title: Read and reconstruct
workbook.prompt: Using 1 for black and 0 for white, draw width 3, height 2 with rows 1,0,1 and 0,1,0. Read it back into numbers and count black pixels.
workbook.answer: The upper row has black, white, black; the lower row has white, black, white. Reading back gives the supplied two rows. There are three black pixels among six total positions.

workbook.title: Preserve the missing field
workbook.prompt: A message contains 1,0,0,1,1,0 but gives no dimensions. Show a one-row arrangement and a two-row arrangement using the same values. Name the extra information that would distinguish them.
workbook.answer: One row of width 6 is [1,0,0,1,1,0]. Two rows of width 3 are [1,0,0] and [1,1,0]. Specify width and height, plus reading order and colour convention. The values alone do not choose the shape.

workbook.title: Test a count feature
workbook.prompt: A classifier receives only the number of black pixels. Can it always distinguish the chapter's cross from every other three by three pattern? Construct a different pattern with the same count and explain.
workbook.answer: No. Rows [1,1,1], [1,1,0], [0,0,0] have five black pixels, as does the cross, but a different arrangement. The classifier receives identical input counts for the two, so that feature alone cannot distinguish them.

workbook.title: Design a new counterexample
workbook.prompt: Create two different images of width 4 and height 2, each with exactly three black pixels. Write both complete row encodings. Explain which fact their shared count retains and which difference it discards.
workbook.answer: One valid pair is A [1,1,1,0]/[0,0,0,0] and B [1,0,0,0]/[0,1,0,1]. Both have two rows of four values and three ones. Count retains the number of black positions but discards their locations. Other valid pairs are accepted if dimensions, counts and arrangements meet the constraints.

workbook.title: Locate an input problem
workbook.prompt: A program receives the correct grid but displays black wherever the code says 0 and white wherever it says 1. A student proposes collecting more classifier examples. Identify the earlier mismatch and the first check to perform.
workbook.answer: The display uses the opposite colour convention from the sender. Check and align the encoding/decoding convention, then reconstruct a known grid. More classifier examples would not be the first repair for this identified input/display mismatch.

teacher.background: The image is binary for transparency, not a claim that ordinary colour images contain only zeros and ones as pixel values. Distinguish bit-level storage from the image value convention. Grid reconstruction is assessed separately from interpretation. A learner may name the worked pattern differently while still reconstructing it correctly.
materials: Squared paper and a dark pencil for each learner
The worked grid with its explicit reading convention
Two empty two-row four-column grids for independent assessment
sessions: Recall the tied-threshold example. Ask why indistinguishable evidence can leave different answers possible.
Agree on colour and reading conventions. Reconstruct the worked grid row by row.
Flatten the values and show why dimensions matter. Compare the two five-black-pixel patterns.
Pairs complete W1 and W2, exchanging encodings and reading them back.
Show two equal-count grids and ask which input a count-only classifier would receive.
Complete W3 and diagnose a reversed convention. Require a specific counterexample.
Collect W4 independently. Check the dimensions and counts before evaluating the explanation.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Distinguish stored values from assigned meaning.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The two rows are black-white-black and white-black-white, giving three black pixels. Other arrangements share that count, so it cannot recover positions. For the exit, move one black pixel to a previously white position while preserving the total; the image changes but the count does not.
misconceptions: The number one always means black
Our convention states that meaning. Other encodings use different scales or channels; read their specification.
A pixel count is the picture
Have students reconstruct two different arrangements with the same count.
A grid decoder only reconstructs the representation. A separate interpretation step assigns a category.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both images are two by four, each has three ones, the patterns differ and the explanation identifies lost location information. If a learner draws valid pictures but mismatches their code, reteach the round-trip check, then assess with fresh patterns.
teacher.support: Provide large tactile or printed cells, with numbers as well as shading so colour is unnecessary. Let learners dictate row values. Extension: construct two grids with equal counts in every row but different arrangements, showing that row totals still lose information.
teacher.next: Week 6 transfers the idea of ordered numerical representations to sound, where the positions refer to times rather than image locations.
